sections.content:
Worked via signed-in ChatGPT

2.1 — Agriculture and connected markets
Theory
Understand the idea

Agriculture connects the production of food, fibre and raw materials with the people and businesses that use them. Some agricultural products are consumed within Australia, while others enter international trade. This means agriculture is connected to both domestic and overseas markets.

Agricultural activity includes more than work completed on farms. It also supports connected work in transport, processing and other parts of the supply chain. A supply chain is the series of activities that moves a product from its place of production towards the people or businesses that use it. For example, an agricultural material may need to be transported, processed, stored and distributed before it reaches a market.

Value adding occurs when a raw agricultural material is changed into another product. This can make the material easier to store, transport or use in different ways. Value adding also connects primary production with processing and other businesses. It does not mean that every product follows the same pathway. Different products may require different forms of handling, processing or distribution.

Australian agriculture includes crop, livestock, horticulture, fisheries and forestry activities. These activities contribute different products to communities and markets. The mix of agricultural activity in an area is influenced by environmental and economic factors. Climate, water availability and soil type affect what can be produced successfully. Proximity to markets can also influence which activities are practical because products must reach processors, distributors or consumers.

Australian agriculture is diverse and export-oriented. However, its importance is not limited to trade. Agriculture supplies communities, supports livelihoods and connects regional production with wider markets. These connections give agriculture both economic and social value. Understanding agriculture therefore requires looking beyond the farm gate to the people, businesses and markets linked through the supply chain.

Key takeaways

Agriculture supplies food, fibre and raw materials to domestic and international markets.

Farm production supports connected work in transport, processing and supply chains.

Value adding changes raw materials so they can be stored, transported or used differently.

Agricultural activity varies with climate, water, soil and access to markets.

Knowledge check

Which statement best describes the markets connected to Australian agriculture?
A. Agriculture supplies only nearby communities.
B. Agriculture connects domestic consumption with international trade.
C. Agriculture produces only goods for overseas markets.
D. Agriculture is separate from consumer markets.

Answer: B. Agriculture connects domestic consumption with international trade.
Correct feedback: Correct. The theory explains that agricultural products are used within Australia and also enter international trade.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Agriculture is connected to both Australian consumers and overseas markets.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Why does agricultural activity support work beyond farms?
A. Products often move through transport, processing and other supply-chain activities.
B. Every farm operates its own international shipping business.
C. Agricultural products are always sold directly where they are produced.
D. Only processed products require workers.

Answer: A. Products often move through transport, processing and other supply-chain activities.
Correct feedback: Correct. Agriculture supports connected work as products move through the supply chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory identifies transport, processing and other supply-chain activities as connected work.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

What is a supply chain?
A. A list of crops grown in one area
B. A set of rules for choosing farm machinery
C. The activities that move a product from production towards its users
D. A type of international market

Answer: C. The activities that move a product from production towards its users
Correct feedback: Correct. A supply chain links production with the people or businesses that use the product.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the sequence of activities between production and use.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Which example best represents value adding?
A. Leaving a raw material unchanged at its place of production
B. Changing a raw agricultural material into a product that can be used differently
C. Choosing a farm because it is close to a town
D. Comparing rainfall between two regions

Answer: B. Changing a raw agricultural material into a product that can be used differently
Correct feedback: Correct. Value adding changes a raw agricultural material into another useful product.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Value adding requires the raw material to be changed in some way.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

What can value adding help an agricultural product do?
A. Avoid all transport and storage
B. Become easier to store, transport or use in different ways
C. Grow successfully in every climate
D. Remain separate from processing businesses

Answer: B. Become easier to store, transport or use in different ways
Correct feedback: Correct. The theory identifies storage, transport and different uses as possible benefits of value adding.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory explains several practical ways that changing a raw material can affect its use.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Which group contains only agricultural activity areas named in the theory?
A. Mining, construction, tourism and banking
B. Crops, livestock, horticulture, fisheries and forestry
C. Retail, aviation, medicine and software
D. Manufacturing, education, housing and entertainment

Answer: B. Crops, livestock, horticulture, fisheries and forestry
Correct feedback: Correct. These five activity areas are identified as parts of Australian agriculture.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Return to the paragraph describing the diversity of Australian agriculture.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Which factor can influence the mix of agricultural activity in an area?
A. Climate, water availability, soil type and proximity to markets
B. The colour of nearby buildings
C. The number of school subjects offered locally
D. The style of packaging used by all businesses

Answer: A. Climate, water availability, soil type and proximity to markets
Correct feedback: Correct. These environmental and economic factors influence what activities are practical.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory names environmental conditions and access to markets as key influences.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Why can proximity to markets affect agricultural activity?
A. Products may need to reach processors, distributors or consumers.
B. Markets control the climate and soil type.
C. All agricultural products must be used where they are produced.
D. Farms can operate only inside large cities.

Answer: A. Products may need to reach processors, distributors or consumers.
Correct feedback: Correct. Access to markets matters because products must move to the next users in the supply chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about where products may need to travel after production.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

What does it mean to describe Australian agriculture as diverse?
A. It includes different agricultural activities that contribute different products.
B. It produces only one type of raw material.
C. Every region carries out exactly the same activities.
D. It is limited to livestock production.

Answer: A. It includes different agricultural activities that contribute different products.
Correct feedback: Correct. Diversity refers to the range of activities and products within agriculture.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory links agricultural diversity to several different activity areas and products.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Why does agriculture have both economic and social value?
A. It supplies communities, supports livelihoods and links regional production to wider markets.
B. It removes the need for transport and processing.
C. It guarantees that every region produces the same goods.
D. It matters only when products are exported.

Answer: A. It supplies communities, supports livelihoods and links regional production to wider markets.
Correct feedback: Correct. These contributions show how agriculture supports both economic activity and communities.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory explains that agriculture matters for communities, livelihoods and market connections, not only trade.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain how an agricultural product can connect farm production with wider markets through a supply chain.
Scaffold:

Identify at least two activities that may occur after production.

Explain how these activities help move the product towards users or businesses.

Appropriate response example: An agricultural product may be transported from its place of production and then processed, stored or distributed. These supply-chain activities connect the farm with processors, businesses and consumers in domestic or international markets.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Prompt: Explain why different parts of Australia may have different types of agricultural activity.
Scaffold:

Name two environmental or market factors from the theory.

Explain how these factors can influence what is practical to produce.

Appropriate response example: Agricultural activity can differ because areas have different climates, water availability and soil types. Proximity to markets also matters because products may need to reach processors, distributors or consumers. These factors influence which crop, livestock, horticulture, fisheries or forestry activities are practical.
Source: Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Source boundary

This section explains agricultural contribution, supply-chain connections, value adding and links between regional production and wider markets. It does not use stale numerical statistics, percentages, rankings, destinations or current export-market figures from the lesson.

Sources

Agriculture and connected markets lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

sections.title: The four dimensions of food security
sections.content:
Worked via signed-in ChatGPT

2.2 — The four dimensions of food security
Theory
Understand the idea

Food security exists when people have reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that supports an active, healthy life. Food security is not only about how much food is produced. It depends on four connected dimensions: availability, access, utilisation and stability.

Availability concerns whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present. Food may be available through production, stored supplies and wider supply systems. However, food being present in a country or community does not automatically mean that every person can obtain it.

Access concerns whether people have the physical and economic resources needed to obtain suitable food. Physical access can be affected by whether food can reach people through transport and supply networks. Economic access depends on whether people have the resources required to obtain the food that is available. A country may have a large food supply while some households still lack access to it.

Utilisation concerns whether food and other conditions allow nutritional needs to be met. It includes the quality and variety of the diet, as well as the influence of clean water, sanitation and health. Food may be available and accessible, but poor conditions affecting utilisation can still prevent people from gaining its full nutritional value.

Stability means that availability, access and utilisation continue over time without a high risk of interruption or loss. A food supply may be available and accessible for a short period but still be unstable if those conditions cannot continue. Stability therefore applies across the other three dimensions rather than acting separately from them.

All four dimensions must work together for food security to exist. Strong availability alone is not enough if people cannot access food. Access alone is not enough if food cannot be utilised to meet nutritional needs. Conditions must also remain stable over time. Examining the four dimensions together provides a clearer understanding of why food security can differ between countries, communities and households.

Key takeaways

Food security requires reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.

Availability concerns whether enough suitable food is present through production, stocks and supply.

Access and utilisation affect whether people can obtain food and meet nutritional needs.

Stability means the other food-security dimensions continue over time.

Knowledge check

Which statement best describes food security?
A. Food is produced in large quantities, even if people cannot obtain it.
B. People have reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
C. Every household grows all of its own food.
D. Food is available for a short period during the year.

Answer: B. People have reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
Correct feedback: Correct. Food security requires reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Food security includes access, quality, sufficiency and reliability, not production alone.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

What does the availability dimension of food security examine?
A. Whether people understand food labels
B. Whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present
C. Whether every person eats the same diet
D. Whether food remains affordable for one household

Answer: B. Whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present
Correct feedback: Correct. Availability concerns whether sufficient food of suitable quality is present.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on whether food is present through production, stored supplies and supply systems.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Which group is identified as contributing to food availability?
A. Production, stored supplies and wider supply systems
B. Diet, exercise and personal preferences
C. Income, advertising and packaging
D. Sanitation, health and cooking skills

Answer: A. Production, stored supplies and wider supply systems
Correct feedback: Correct. The theory identifies production, stored supplies and supply systems as sources of availability.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Return to the sentence explaining how food may be made available.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

What does the access dimension mainly concern?
A. Whether food can be stored for several years
B. Whether people have the physical and economic resources to obtain suitable food
C. Whether enough food is produced nationally
D. Whether all food has the same nutritional value

Answer: B. Whether people have the physical and economic resources to obtain suitable food
Correct feedback: Correct. Access concerns the physical and economic resources needed to obtain food.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Access is about people's ability to obtain available food.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Why can food be available while some households still experience food insecurity?
A. Available food is always unsuitable for people.
B. Households may lack the physical or economic resources needed to obtain it.
C. Food availability prevents supply networks from operating.
D. Food security applies only to countries, not households.

Answer: B. Households may lack the physical or economic resources needed to obtain it.
Correct feedback: Correct. Availability does not guarantee that every household has access to the food.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory separates the presence of food from people's ability to obtain it.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

What does utilisation examine?
A. How exports are ranked between countries
B. How food, diet, clean water, sanitation and health affect nutritional needs
C. How quickly food is transported to shops
D. How much land is used for production

Answer: B. How food, diet, clean water, sanitation and health affect nutritional needs
Correct feedback: Correct. Utilisation considers whether food and surrounding conditions allow nutritional needs to be met.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the conditions that affect whether the body can gain nutritional value from food.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Which situation best shows a problem with utilisation?
A. Food is present, but conditions prevent people from gaining its full nutritional value.
B. Food is stored before being transported.
C. People have enough resources to obtain suitable food.
D. Production and supply continue reliably over time.

Answer: A. Food is present, but conditions prevent people from gaining its full nutritional value.
Correct feedback: Correct. Utilisation can be limited even when food is available and accessible.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look for the situation where food is present but nutritional needs may still not be met.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

What does stability mean in food security?
A. Only food production remains unchanged.
B. The other dimensions continue over time without a high risk of interruption or loss.
C. People obtain food once, regardless of what happens later.
D. All food is stored in one location.

Answer: B. The other dimensions continue over time without a high risk of interruption or loss.
Correct feedback: Correct. Stability means availability, access and utilisation continue over time.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Stability is about the continuation of the other dimensions, not a single event.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Why might a food supply be accessible but not stable?
A. It is available only through production.
B. People can obtain it now, but access may not continue over time.
C. It contains safe and nutritious food.
D. It is supported by clean water and sanitation.

Answer: B. People can obtain it now, but access may not continue over time.
Correct feedback: Correct. Short-term access does not guarantee that access will continue.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Compare conditions that exist briefly with conditions that can be maintained.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Why must all four dimensions be considered together?
A. Each dimension describes a separate type of farming.
B. Strong performance in one dimension does not guarantee food security.
C. Availability automatically creates access, utilisation and stability.
D. Stability replaces the need for the other three dimensions.

Answer: B. Strong performance in one dimension does not guarantee food security.
Correct feedback: Correct. Food security can fail when even one connected dimension is weak.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The final paragraph explains why no single dimension is enough by itself.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain how food can be available in a country while some households still lack food security.
Scaffold:

Define availability in your response.

Explain how limited physical or economic access can affect households.

Appropriate response example: Availability means that sufficient food of suitable quality is present through production, stocks or supply. Some households may still lack food security if they do not have the physical or economic resources needed to obtain that food.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Prompt: Explain why stability is connected to the other three dimensions of food security.
Scaffold:

Name the three dimensions that must continue over time.

Explain why short-term conditions are not enough for food security.

Appropriate response example: Stability means that availability, access and utilisation continue over time without a high risk of interruption or loss. Food may be present and accessible for a short time, but food security is not stable if those conditions cannot continue.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

Source boundary

This section teaches the four dimensions of food security and explains how they work together. It does not use numerical Australian production claims, statistics, rankings, dates, personal medical advice or dietary advice.

Sources

The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Food security concepts and measurement: https://www.fao.org/4/j0710e/j0710e.htm

sections.content:

2.3 — Threats and resilient responses
Theory
Understand the idea

Food systems can face pressures that affect production, transport, availability and prices. These pressures include drought and water scarcity, climate change and extreme weather, soil degradation, trade or supply-chain disruption, and pest or disease outbreaks. Different threats affect food systems in different ways, so responses need to match the problem.

Drought and water scarcity can reduce the water available to crops and livestock. Extreme weather and changing conditions can also disrupt production and damage transport connections. Even when food has been produced, supply-chain disruption can slow or prevent its movement. This can affect where food is available and what people may need to pay for it.

Soil degradation is another long-term threat. When soil condition declines, the soil may become less able to support future production. Soil conservation is therefore an important conceptual response because it aims to protect the productive capacity of the land over time.

Pests and diseases can harm plants, animals, people or the environment. Biosecurity reduces these risks by helping prevent, detect and manage harmful pests and diseases. Monitoring and planning also support food systems by identifying possible problems and preparing responses before or during disruption.

Resilience means preparing for disruption, adapting when conditions change, and continuing or recovering essential food-system functions. Conceptual responses can include careful water management, soil conservation, diverse production and supply pathways, biosecurity, monitoring and planning. Diverse pathways can reduce dependence on one source, route or method, although they do not remove every risk.

A suitable response must match the threat. Water management may help address water scarcity, while biosecurity is more closely connected to pest and disease risks. Responses can also involve trade-offs, such as requiring extra resources, planning or changes to existing systems. No single response can remove every threat. A resilient food system uses several connected approaches and adjusts them as risks and conditions change.

Key takeaways

Food systems face threats from environmental, biological and supply-chain disruptions.

Different threats can affect production, transport, availability and prices.

Resilience involves preparing, adapting, continuing and recovering essential functions.

Responses must match the threat, and no single response removes every risk.

Knowledge check

Which group contains only threats to food systems identified in the theory?
A. Drought, soil degradation, supply-chain disruption and pest outbreaks
B. Packaging design, advertising, cooking styles and tourism
C. School timetables, housing design, sport and entertainment
D. Road colour, shop layout, clothing and furniture

Answer: A. Drought, soil degradation, supply-chain disruption and pest outbreaks
Correct feedback: Correct. These are all identified pressures that can affect food systems.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph for the authorised list of food-system threats.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

How can drought and water scarcity affect agricultural production?
A. They can reduce the water available to crops and livestock.
B. They always improve soil condition.
C. They prevent all pest and disease outbreaks.
D. They guarantee stable transport routes.

Answer: A. They can reduce the water available to crops and livestock.
Correct feedback: Correct. Drought and water scarcity can limit the water available for crops and livestock.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the direct effect of reduced water availability.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

How can extreme weather affect a food system?
A. It can disrupt production and transport connections.
B. It affects only the appearance of food packaging.
C. It always increases soil quality.
D. It removes the need for planning.

Answer: A. It can disrupt production and transport connections.
Correct feedback: Correct. Extreme weather can interrupt both production and the movement of food.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory links extreme weather with two major parts of the food system.
Source: The Value of Agriculture and Food Security lesson:  https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1yxBn4_4WELDwKOtz-DuUKyaDwEA6iiO9yl-zjA0Tbxc/edit; Why Australia needs a National Food Security Strategy: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/food/national-food-security-strategy/why-we-need-a-food-security-strategy; Snapshot of Australian agriculture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/products/insights/snapshot-of-australian-agriculture

Why can supply-chain disruption cause problems even when food has already been produced?
A. It can affect the movement, availability and prices of food.
B. It changes all food into raw materials.
C. It prevents soil from supporting crops.
D. It automatically causes a disease outbreak.

Answer: A. It can affect the movement, availability and prices of food.
Correct feedback: Correct. Produced food still needs to move through supply pathways to reach markets and consumers.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about what happens after production when transport or distribution is interrupted.

What is a possible long-term effect of soil degradation?
A. The soil may become less able to support future production.
B. Transport routes become more reliable.
C. Water availability always increases.
D. Pest risks disappear completely.

Answer: A. The soil may become less able to support future production.
Correct feedback: Correct. Soil degradation can reduce the soil's productive capacity over time.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the relationship between soil condition and future production.

A. To reduce risks from harmful pests and diseases
B. To increase dependence on one supply route
C. To replace all soil conservation
D. To prevent every type of extreme weather

Answer: A. To reduce risks from harmful pests and diseases
Correct feedback: Correct. Biosecurity helps reduce risks from pests and diseases that may cause harm.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Biosecurity is connected specifically to biological threats.

Which statement best describes resilience?
A. Avoiding all change in a food system
B. Preparing for disruption, adapting, and continuing or recovering essential functions
C. Using one response for every possible threat
D. Producing food without transport or supply pathways

Answer: B. Preparing for disruption, adapting, and continuing or recovering essential functions
Correct feedback: Correct. Resilience involves preparation, adaptation, continuation and recovery.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Resilience does not mean removing all change or using one fixed response.

A. They can reduce dependence on one source, route or method.
B. They guarantee that no disruption will occur.
C. They remove the need for monitoring and planning.

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain how a supply-chain disruption can affect food security even when food has already been produced.
Scaffold:

Identify what part of the food system is disrupted.

Explain how this can affect movement, availability or prices.

Appropriate response example: A supply-chain disruption can interrupt the transport or distribution of food after production. This may stop food reaching some places, reduce its availability and affect prices even though the food has already been produced.

Prompt: Explain why a resilient food system needs several responses rather than one solution.
Scaffold:

Name two different threats from the theory.

Match each threat with a suitable conceptual response and explain the connection.

Appropriate response example: Food systems face different threats, so one response cannot address them all. Careful water management can respond to drought and water scarcity, while biosecurity addresses pest and disease risks. Soil conservation, diverse supply pathways, monitoring and planning can also support resilience, but each response has limits and possible trade-offs.
